So I've always had ultra liberal parents, and never had the chance to use a gun besides only 3 times in my life with family members at shooting ranges.

So what would be a good gun to get?

I'd prefer something simple to operate, reasonable stopping power, and small enough to conceal carry.
Wanting to purchase my first ever handgun for concealed carry - advice for a newbie?

The problem is, a firearm easy to conceal is not typically a good firearm for a beginner. I would stay away from a subcompact like a SigSauer 938 and go for something a little larger. For simplicity sake you cant go wrong with a revolver.
Most ranges have rental guns, go and try out a few and find out what is most comfortable to you. When you finally do decide, practice with that weapon.

Agreed. Go try a Glock 19, Glock 17, Smith & Wesson M&P9, Sig Sauer P320, P229 or P226, Springfield XD, try at least one revolver. Pick up as many as you can and feel them in your hand and shoot them. Ask them to let you try guns with and without an external safety. Start with 9mm for callber, which should be the first handgun caliber anyone goes with if it's for self defense. It might also be your last caliber as there really is no need for anything more than 9mm.

A revolver is simple-Simon. They're fairly simple, mechanically. Don't fall for the myth that you'll need more than 6 rounds for self defense. A snubby in .38 spc or .357 mag would be more than suitable. IWB holsters are the way to go for concealing those comfortably. OR... a small auto in .380 for deep concealment. Bersa makes a very affordable .380 that's really good for that.

Remember that marksmanship and felt recoil should take second when it comes to self-defense handguns, as the reactionary gap would be so close as to negate the use of a marksman's "sight picture", nor the thought of many shots at the range hurting your hand would even factor.

Tune yourself into the signage you see around the entryways at businesses to see who "exercises their property rights" barring entry for those non-LEO gun bearers.

Don't forget to bring (and mount, if possible) a lockbox in your car for those occasions that you my have to enter an establishment that bars firearms. These kinds of boxes are typically $50-$150, depending on their features. Hornady makes a nice one that has a bar that'll extend to hook around a strut or seat frame.
You can't be serious about Bersa. The smallest .380 they make is PPK sized. I would understand if you said Kahr CW380.
Yep. Bersa. Affordable. I just speak from my experience... favored over un-experience and gun reviews.

I think the only correct answer is to take a CCW class. One immediate advantage is that they will usually have a variety of guns that you can try, which makes that part of the process easy.

The main reason to take the class is that you need to know the law, and its complicated. Depending on your state, it matters a lot how you handle things like traffic stops, or going to a restaurant that also serves alcohol, or carry into your workplace. You also need to know the law about using your gun for self defense - you probably have a duty to retreat when possible (when outside your home) and if you don't understand the consequences of this, you can go to jail for what seemed like a perfectly reasonable act.

Any local gun shop should be able to direct you to a CCW class, and the bigger shops often hold their own. Take the best class you can find in your area, try all the guns, and then decide.
Yes on the legal aspect, but in my locale the courses are useless for the gun selection. Usually you have to bring the one you qualify with.

Have a look at this book, it has a decent chapter on the selection principles: amazon dot com/Defensive-Pistol-Fundamentals-Grant-Cunningham/dp/1440242801/

You have to be compatible with the gun. For example, I like everything about Springfield XD-S, but when I shoot it, the significant undercut of its trigger guard hurts my knuckle badly. Nobody else seem to have this problem, because the shape of their hands is different.

Alternatively, just go out and buy Glock 19, go and practice with it a lot. Once you got used to it, you can explore the space and find a gun that's better for you: slimmer or thicker, lighter or heavier, or in a different caliber. There's really no way to buy the best gun right away, so don't try to accomplish it.

Get a M&P Shield 9mm with no thumb safety. They are like $215AR which is a goddam steal. Then buy 3-4 holsters and a gun belt, thicker and stronger than standard belts. That's another $75. Return the holsters you don't like, carry that for 6 months, swapping things around as they feel uncomfortable.

After 6 months you will have a great idea of what you can get away with, what size pistol you like, what holster style, what works with you clothes, and allows you to draw well. Keep the shield as a cheap stash/trunk gun and buy what you really want in the $400-$700 range, or keep mainlining the Shield.

Personally I like cheap, RELIABLE, but cheap carry guns. Hurts less when the police make you drop it, kick it across the pavement, bag it, never give it back.
